title: Five Questions Every Dentist Should Ask Their Financial Advisor
html:
Written by: John F. Reutemann, Jr., CLU, CFP®
(Founder and CEO, Financial and Wealth Advisor, Research Financial Strategies)

You spend years mastering clinical skills, running your practice, and taking care of patients. More than likely, you have very little time or desire to become an investing expert and manage your retirement savings. Instead, you probably ask friends, family members, and colleagues for advice and a referral to their financial planner.

This is where problems can arise.

Does this sound familiar? With your busy schedule, you trust the financial planner whom your best friend or associate uses, hand over your money, and then check your statements (when you find the time to do so). You review the data. Everything looks fine, so you assume nothing is wrong… month after month and year after year. Well, did you know that this lack of a relationship with your financial advisor could quietly cost you tens of thousands or even hundreds of thousands of dollars over the course of your career?

Specifically, the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority’s year-end 2025 statistics show that “625 new disciplinary cases [were] filed,” and “the amount of fines and disgorgement rose year-over-year by 31.7% to $99.6 million from $75.6 million.” (1)

Why does this happen? It can result from high fees you may be unaware of, mediocre performance, and/or a retirement plan that was not built with your specific situation, goals, and best interests in mind. If this is making you nervous about your nest egg, it should, and it’s time to pay attention. Start with a few questions related to the top issues I see most often with dentists and small business owners.

What Are the Top 5 Questions You Should Ask Your Financial Advisor Right Now?

1. What are your credentials?

The first place to start is with the advisor’s own credentials, even if that advisor is a friend. Is the advisor a true fee-based fiduciary with a Series 65 license, or is he or she a broker receiving commissions on product sales? This is not a technicality. A fiduciary is legally required to act in your best interest. A broker is generally held to a lower “suitability” standard and can be paid more to sell you one product over another, which may not be the better choice for you.

In fact, the Securities and Exchange Commission notes that investment advisers have a fiduciary duty. “Section 206 of the Advisers Act establishes ‘federal fiduciary standards’ to govern the conduct of investment advisers.” (2) In contrast, “broker-dealers follow the SEC’s Regulation Best Interest, not a fiduciary standard.” (3)

Ask directly how your advisor is licensed and how he or she is paid. Then, get that answer in writing.

2. Should you choose a financial advisor because they’re your friend?

If you have a friend who works in finance, it doesn’t mean they need to be your financial advisor. Friendship is not a credential. Just because you have a personal relationship with your advisor, this should never stop you from asking the same hard questions you would ask a stranger.

3. What software packages do you use?

This is something you would probably never think of asking. No matter what your age, the questions about your financial situation and retirement change regularly, but the need for a clear, complete picture never does. This is where the software packages your advisor uses come in. They need to keep track of everything you own and its performance. If your current advisor does not use comprehensive planning software, that may be an indication that you have the wrong advisor.

Without a real-time, consolidated view of every account, including investments, retirement accounts, insurance, and cash, neither you nor your advisor can truly see the full picture… and you cannot manage what you cannot see.

And remember, even with the right software in place, a plan is only as good as how often it is reviewed, which brings me to…

4. Are you keeping score?

At a minimum, I highly suggest that you have an account review every 90 days. It does not have to be in person. A phone call or online meeting works just as well, given how busy you are at your dental practice. But it’s essential to add this to your schedule so that your advisor can review the performance of each of your accounts with you relative to their benchmarks and keep you informed about what’s going on.

If you don’t have at least quarterly reviews, receive vague data you don’t understand, or skip the benchmark comparison altogether, you have no real way of knowing whether your money is working as hard as it should be or whether you are simply being told that everything is fine.

5. Are you making the maximum contribution you’re eligible for in your 401(k) or self-employed retirement plan? And again, where is it?

Finally, look closely at your retirement plan itself. Many small dental practice owners have their 401(k) with an insurance company. In my opinion, that is not the best or least expensive option, and it often comes with higher embedded costs than you may realize. Here’s an example from the U.S. Department of Labor:

“Assume that you are an employee with 35 years until retirement and a current 401(k) account balance of $25,000. If returns on investments in your account over the next 35 years average 7 percent and fees and expenses reduce your average returns by 0.5 percent, your account balance will grow to $227,000 at retirement, even if there are no further contributions to your account. If fees and expenses are 1.5 percent, however, your account balance will grow to only $163,000. The 1 percent difference in fees and expenses would reduce your account balance at retirement by 28 percent.” (4)

Just because you are small doesn’t mean you can’t have the best, lowest-cost plan. But someone needs to take the time to look, compare the fees, and make the change.

You Don’t Need to Be a Financial Expert

You just need to pay attention to your investments and ask questions. Talk to the person managing your money and get real answers. Ensure they have experience and the right credentials. Ask about your custodian, how and when you receive data and reports, fees, how your investments align with your specific goals, and other key questions so that you know what’s going on.

And it’s never too late to start. If you have been on autopilot with your financial advisor for years, it’s time to take action. Remember, when you hand your money over to a manager, that is just the beginning of the relationship. It’s your responsibility to know what’s happening with your investments relative to your goals and why. Otherwise, when you’re ready to retire, you may be in for a big surprise, with fewer funds than expected and more time ahead over the chair!
